Where it began

Ashish Nehra was born in Delhi on 29 April 1979 and was hooked on cricket from boyhood. He and Virender Sehwag, another Delhi lad with big plans, used to ride scooters together to the Feroz Shah Kotla ground so they could get a game. The journeys paid off for both of them. Nehra worked his way up through the city's cricket and into the Delhi side in the Ranji Trophy.

The player

His Test debut came against Sri Lanka in 1999, and he went on to play 17 Tests up to 2004. He took 44 wickets at 42.41, with a best of 4 for 72, and held 4 catches.

The one-day game was where he made his loudest noise. At the 2003 World Cup he took 6 for 23 against England, the best figures by an Indian bowler at a World Cup for the next twenty years, until Mohammad Shami bettered them in 2023. He shared in the 2002 Champions Trophy, which India and Sri Lanka won jointly, and he was part of the squad that won the 2011 World Cup, though he sat out the final.

What made him special

He lasted. He signed off on 1 November 2017 with a Twenty20 international against New Zealand, played at the same Feroz Shah Kotla he had once scootered to as a boy. In between he kept adapting, and at the 2016 T20 World Cup the ICC named him in its team of the tournament. At home he could be just as sharp: in the 2013–14 Ranji Trophy his 6 for 16 bowled Vidarbha out for 88.

Batting was not his department: his 77 Test runs came at 5.50, with a top score of 19. Then again, nobody ever picked him for those.

Away from the middle

He played IPL cricket for Mumbai Indians and later Chennai Super Kings. Once his playing days were over, he moved straight into coaching. Royal Challengers Bangalore made him their bowling coach in January 2018, and he carried on there for the 2019 season.

In January 2022 he became head coach of the brand-new Gujarat Titans. In their very first season they topped the table and then beat Rajasthan Royals in the final, so Nehra became the first IPL-winning head coach from India.

And finally

Not many careers come full circle quite so neatly. The boy who rode to Feroz Shah Kotla by scooter with Sehwag said goodbye to international cricket on that same ground, and then went off to win a trophy in a tracksuit instead of whites.
